name: Hana Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a usual factory shift involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am forty-three and run the sleeve-labelling machine in a drink bottling factory. I left school after secondary school and am still learning to set the heat tunnel; the lead operator checks my first bottles for wrinkled labels. I use an AI assistant every day to explain fault codes, but check its suggestion against the machine book. My wage is low, we have less than one month of expenses saved, and only a few similar plants are nearby. My partner and I have two children at school and a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the shift a helpful fault explanation still leaves us to check the first bottle. The heat tunnel can shrink a label crooked even when the screen looks tidy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ordinary lost overtime already worries me. My low wage and less than a month saved leave our mortgage exposed, and the few nearby bottling plants are not a quick escape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep running the labeller and checking first bottles with the lead. I would put a new small amount from each full paid week into an emergency account after mortgage, food and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about our narrow margin even in a quiet AI picture. A stable machine does not turn a low wage into a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you see on the first bottle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I check whether the sleeve sits straight over the cap and whether the date is visible. If it wrinkles in the tunnel, I stop the belt before the tray fills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What amount could you actually put aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some weeks it would be only a few coins. I would transfer new money only after the mortgage and groceries are paid, and record the amount rather than guess.

The **familiar** AI fault explanation still needs a physical label check.
think: A **low** wage and little cash make the mortgage vulnerable to lost overtime.
**Few** nearby bottling plants limit my fallback.
do: **Keep** running sleeve labeller and checking first bottles with lead.
**Save** new money from full wages after mortgage and groceries.
feel: **Anxious** about a thin household margin despite steady production.
S0.quote: A stable machine does not turn a low wage into a cushion.
fieldNote: **Hana** uses AI daily for fault codes but verifies them against a machine book and physical bottles.
Her **baseline** anxiety follows low pay, thin savings, a mortgage and few local alternatives.

steps.text: Keep running sleeve labeller and check first bottles with lead
Save new money from full wages after essential bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AI may plan bottle orders faster, but a machine still needs a person to catch a bad sleeve. I would volunteer for a new AI tunnel-temperature alert only if the plant offers paid practice with the belt safely stopped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If planning gets faster, managers might trim my paid changeover minutes. Our mortgage cannot absorb many shorter weeks, even if I learn a useful alert quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the labeller shifts and ask for the paid setup target in writing. If an offered paid stopped-line slot appears, I would learn the new alert controls and compare them with real first bottles; after sustained hour cuts, I would apply only to a posted nearby operator opening that covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a real loss of paid minutes. Learning quickly helps me respond, but it does not pay a missed mortgage instalment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you test the alert?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare its temperature warning with the date and seam on ten first bottles. If a sleeve is wrong while the alert says green, I would keep the manual check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you apply elsewhere?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after cut hours show on repeated rotas and an actual nearby opening pays enough for mortgage, food and travel. I cannot swap a known wage for a hiring rumour.

say: I would **try** a new AI tunnel alert in offered paid safe practice.
I would **ask** for written paid setup time before faster schedules become targets.
think: A **thin** cushion makes even a small recurring wage cut serious each week.
do: **Learn** new AI alert in offered paid stopped-line practice.
**Apply** after repeated cuts to posted nearby bill-covering operator role.
S1.quote: Our mortgage cannot absorb many shorter weeks, even if I learn a useful alert quickly.
fieldNote: Her **adaptive** plan involves actual conditional learning of a new AI alert, beyond daily fault explanations.
The **job** application retains repeated cuts, a posted nearby opening and a household-sustaining wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI reaches orders in 2028 when I am forty-five, then capable hands-on robots reach bottle handling around 2031 when I am forty-eight. A robot could feed and clear the labeller without a junior operator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of my paid labeller hours to go if that robot works. We have less than a month saved, two children and a mortgage; I lie awake adding the missing wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid shifts while asking for a fully funded machine-maintenance course on paid time with safe isolated-line practice. I would enrol only if a posted nearby maintenance job accepts it and pays our bills, then apply after qualifying; if robots cut shifts first, I would stop paid outings and apply to posted nearby operator jobs at adequate pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed by an expected large wage loss and nights spent on the mortgage. A course route is possible, but no place or vacancy is promised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the course teach you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need to isolate the labeller, test a sensor and restart under a qualified fitter. My secondary schooling and operator practice do not make me a maintenance technician yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which outing would stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cinema would go before the children’s school meals or mortgage payment. It saves little against a whole wage, but I can do it immediately.

I would **seek** paid maintenance training tied to a real nearby job.
think: I **expect** most junior hours to disappear and lie awake over the mortgage.

do: **Enrol** in funded paid-time safe maintenance training only if a posted nearby bill-covering job accepts the qualification.
**Apply** after qualifying to posted nearby maintenance job covering bills.

feel: **Alarmed** by expected major wage loss and sleepless mortgage worry.

fieldNote: Her **alarm** follows an expected large labeller-hour cut and explicit sleeplessness.
**Training** and application require funding, paid time, safe practice, accepted qualification and a posted adequate local job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI reaches orders in 2031 when I am forty-eight, and capable robots handle bottles around 2034 when I am fifty-one. Five paid years give us room to prepare before the labeller itself changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could still lose routine hours, but I might qualify for maintenance while drawing wages. Our current cash is thin, so unpaid study would make the family weaker before any robot arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the labeller job and save new money from each full pay packet after bills. If the plant funds a maintenance course with paid study and safe practice, and a posted nearby role accepts the certificate at bill-covering pay, I would enrol and apply after qualifying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about later cuts, with more control than in the fast case. I can use the extra years only while the shifts stay paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why maintenance rather than another bottling line?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The same robots could reach other lines too. A sensor and drive still need safe fault finding for a while, though I would not call that permanent protection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course takes unpaid days?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the labeller shifts and decline for now. The mortgage comes before a certificate, however useful the lessons sound.

say: I would **use** paid years for a real maintenance qualification.
think: **Routine** hours remain at risk, but five years allow preparation.
**Funding**, paid days and a posted adequate local role must line up.
do: **Save** new money from full labeller wages after bills.
**Enrol** in funded paid-time safe maintenance training only if a posted nearby bill-covering job accepts the qualification.
**Apply** after qualifying to posted nearby maintenance job covering bills.
feel: **Anxious** about plausible later cuts, with time to prepare.
S3.quote: The mortgage comes before a certificate, however useful the lessons sound.
fieldNote: **New** saving comes from actual wages, not from relabelling existing cash.
She **refuses** unpaid study and keeps the later application tied to an accepted qualification and adequate local vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI reaches orders in 2036 when I am fifty-three, with capable bottle-handling robots around 2039 when I am fifty-six. A decade is useful, but I still expect to need wages after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The children will be older and the mortgage may be smaller by then, yet I cannot assume it is paid off. A long warning only helps if I build savings and a qualification while work is available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid labeller shifts and put a new amount from each full wage into our reserve. If the plant offers paid stopped-line practice, I would learn a new AI sensor-diagnosis control beyond my current fault-code helper. If it funds a safe maintenance course on paid time and a posted nearby job pays our bills, I would qualify and apply after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about eventual operator hours, but less cornered by the longer notice. I would rather measure a real wage than count on a future promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the new AI diagnosis do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would compare sensor failures across runs and suggest a test, beyond explaining one code. I would verify it on a stopped line with the fitter before changing a part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for a vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would first seek a posted nearby job paying mortgage, travel and food. A distant role would have to cover a real family move; I would not assume our children could simply change schools.

think: A **smaller** mortgage is possible, not guaranteed.
I will **still** need wages when capable robots reach the labeller.
do: **Save** new money from full paid labeller weeks after bills.
**Learn** new AI sensor diagnosis in offered paid stopped-line slot.
**Qualify** in funded paid-time course, then apply to posted nearby adequate role.
feel: **Anxious** about later wage risk, with more time to plan.
S4.quote: I would rather measure a real wage than count on a future promise.
fieldNote: Her **new** AI learning is conditional on offered paid safe practice and differs from daily fault-code use.
**Maintenance** training and separate job application keep funding, paid time, safety and actual adequate local work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 case worries me most because robots could remove most labeller hours around 2031 while our mortgage and school bills remain. Paid maintenance training tied to a real nearby job would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets a paid hour to learn the next bottling machine. I use AI every day and still need the lead to check my first bottles. A fault code is not a wage for my children.

headlineQuote: A fault code is not a wage for my children.
portrait: **Hana**, forty-three, is a junior bottling-line operator with secondary schooling and two children.
Her **low** wage, mortgage, less than one month saved and few nearby plants make lost hours dangerous.
She **uses** AI daily for fault explanations and learns new controls early, with physical checks.
Her **plans** require funded paid safe maintenance training and a posted nearby job that covers household bills.
biggestWorry: **Fast** robots around 2031 could remove most paid labeller hours before Hana builds a month of savings.
whatWouldHelp: **Fully** funded paid-time maintenance training and a posted nearby bill-covering job would give her a route.
